I’m not a policy maker, but off the top of my head:

For starters, I’d have Congress preemptively do what they would probably do post some AI disaster. Something like form a committee of academic researchers, security professionals, and other people who are incentivized to be skeptical and have them investigate the risks posed by the AI we have and what’s cooking. The aim would be take the risks seriously and propose policies that seek to mitigate those risks.

I’d also, make more of an effort to cooperate with governments to establish some treaty-like agreements about how we will use AI in critical areas like warfare. We have these kind of agreements about biological and nuclear weapons. We can have them about AI weapons, too. Maybe this would cool down the arms race atmosphere.

I would establish some kind of central-bank like authority whose members are protected from congressional and executive-branch meddling and whose mandate is to influence the development of AI in a way that’s universally agreed to be good society. Not sure how this would look and what their levers would be, but I think something similar to the Feds mandate to balance employment and inflation, but the AI version, would be worth exploring.

Finally, I wouldn’t wait until AI has replaced people and hyper scalers are sitting on trillions to have a plan for how millions of people are supposed to make a living when they can’t find work anymore because agents and robots are doing the jobs they used to do. I think we’re still a ways away from that reality. But having a framework, better yet policies, in place would probably make people feel a lot better about the development of AI. If everyone knows they’re going to get a UBI check for 5K plus access to a solid state sponsored healthcare plan for them and their immediate family when AI makes us all redundant, I don’t think people would be so apprehensive to AI and data centers.

Again, I’m not a policy maker. I’m sure there are a bunch of externalities that people can point out to poke holes in my ideas. Be my guest.

Sitting around doing what amounts to jack shit while the technology that powers the internet seems increasingly vulnerable to the technology we’re building and distributing as fast as possible definitely is not the way to go.

The credit markets seem concerned about the timing of the AI booms future cash flows. So maybe the invisible hand will take care of the situation for awhile. I just hope the unwinding doesn’t take the rest of the economy down with it.

Either way AI is here to stay. So, even if the bubble burst, when the market inevitably comes back the same issues will be there. Better to get ahead then not.

comment_text.value:
I'll take a crack at this one. I've been using matrix and element for over a decade as my main messenger, and it's great, but it also does suck. I even use it for my business chat. It's pretty much the most popular federated encrypted client right now, and it seems to have taken over XMPP's lead. So here's a nice list/rant about why matrix/element sucks.

1. I spent 15 minutes last month helping my business partner sign onto ElementX on his second phone. He's signed on his PC and his primary phone, but the second phone was very difficult. Basically type username and password, but now you have to verify with emoji. How do you do that? Well, sometimes it pops up on your other clients that a new client needs verification. Sometimes the popup never shows, and there's no way to find it. But we found it eventually. Verify via emoji. Great! Let's do it. Oops, it timed out before he could finish. Apparently it has a super short timer that even I struggle with it. Eventually we gave up and used the recovery key, which worked, but you know many people are going to lose that key since it's not a password they can just memorize. Most other messengers, it's just username, password, and then click the email confirmation link. Boom, easy.

2. Audio/Video calling/conferencing. There are apparently 3(?) different technologies in Element alone, depending on which version of Element (desktop, web, mobile). The "old" one is jitsi. The new p2p one appears to be only available to clients that aren't Element? Or you can only create conference rooms in those other clients (commet?), but you can join them from any client. But then those new rooms are sometimes not join-able from Element clients. They just don't appear in the room list at all. Even clicking a link to the room says it's the wrong "room version", but it's a freshly-created room. So I delete the room and make another new one. But now it's a Jitsi room and it doesn't work in this other Element client (all first-party actual Element clients, and all broken in slightly different ways!). So... it's working now, but only after lots of trial and error and lots of cussing from my business partner. And I have to somehow justify that this is better than using Slack/Discord/whatever corporate thing.

3. The official client is fragmented. On mobile, there is Element (classic) and ElementX. You're _supposed_ to use ElementX, since it's the new one, but ElementX does not have all the features of Element (classic), so you might need the Element (classic) client for those things. But Element (classic) is not getting updated, so you're left in the cold as far as updates and the new features (meaning you might not even be able to cross-verify your clients, or join video calls, spaces, etc.)

4. The official matrix server (synapse) is pretty slow. I hosted a couple small communities (~100 people or so?), and synapse somehow kept getting overloaded and crashing. Maybe it needed more than 4GiB, but that seems kind of silly. There are decent 3rd-party clients (continuwuity is my current favorite), but there's no migration path from one server to another without wiping your entire database and starting fresh. So.... my main homeserver is kind of stuck on synapse.

5. Bridges. Yes, you can bridge anything to anything, but have you actually tried it? Interface is super clunky. You have to run a separate bridge service, make sure it swaps keys with the matrix server via a yaml configuration dance, then talk to the bridge's bot in a dedicated matrix channel with special commands that may or may not get your bridge working. I've used signal, discord, telegram, and irc bridges, and they're all a mess in one way or another. My most recent attempt was with the signal bridge. I made the mistake of enabling end-to-end encryption. One day, the bridge server restarted and lost all its encryption keys. Cool, now all the bridged rooms are dead. So naturally, I delete the bridge service and re-configure it from scratch. Now it doesn't work because its bridge bot username was already taken by the previous instance with the lost encryption keys. And I can't just delete that bridge bot user because _matrix does not allow deleting users ever!_. So now I have broken signal bridge rooms and broken signal bot users that I can't ever delete, even with the admin panel. So naturally I open up a postgresql client and delete them manually. Oops, now my matrix database is broken in ways I cannot even begin to comprehend. Because deleting users is not allowed. So now I just can't have a signal bridge. _maybe_ there's a way to make it work, but I've been programming and sys-admin'ing for over 20 years, and it's just beyond me. I'm going to have to (again!) wipe out my homeserver and start over, losing all my messages and contacts (again!). XMPP had very nice transport services, and Psi+ had a very nice UI for configuring and organizing them.

6. Multi-identity support is lacking in all the official and most community clients. If I have a work account and a personal account, I need to start two separate Element clients. Each one is a hefty electron app, and they all have the same systray icon, so I need to trial+error every time to open the right one to message someone. So far, there's only one client I tried that had proper multi-account, and I think it was commet. It was ok, but I hated that it was a flutter desktop app where every click felt super unresponsive. So I went back to Element. Most XMPP clients have multi-identity built-in. I'm not going to use my work identity for personal chat, just like I'm not going to use my hackernews account to message co-workers.

7. No message auto-deletion. Many people like to claim that Element is more secure than Signal. It is not. If you live in an oppressive country where things you say can easily result in prison or torture, you need more than E2E encryption. You need messages to be gone. You can't trust that your device or your friend's device won't get confiscated and forced to reveal your password. Even the United States has forced device unlocking at the borders. Signal (and Confide, and even Telegram) have automatically deleting messages, so even with the keys, there's nothing to see. Matrix stores messages forever. Aside from some complicated server-side setting, there's no way to automatically delete them. You have to right-click and manually delete EVERY message if you want future privacy. Nobody's going to do that. And I tried enabling the synapse settings for auto-deleting messages, but they didn't work. It seems that feature isn't really tested, or it's documented poorly.

8. The spam/CSAM problem when running a public community. The admin tools are a bit lacking, so without some considerable expertise, it's often not worth even having a community matrix server. So folks just make a discord instead, which has actual moderation tools builtin. Yes, I know there are external moderation tools you can install, but why should that be required?

9. The protocol is too complex to make full-featured 3rd-party clients. This isn't IRC where you can make a basic client in 3 lines of perl. You'll notice that the 3rd-party clients are all lacking in some features of Element, the official client. Even the official ElementX client lacks features of Element Classic. Most folks are stuck on the official electron-based Element client, which has a fairly clunky UX (try explaining to your grandma how to cross-verify clients).

This list is just off the top of my head. I could probably write a whole book on the problems with the matrix ecosystem. But again, matrix is the best we have. IRCv3 hasn't really caught on, and the need for an IRC bouncer to receive offline messages isn't commonly excepted in 2026. XMPP was/is ok, but it hasn't been commonly used since Google Hangouts pulled the bait+switch on us 10+. I keep thinking I should really just go back to XMPP, or start using delta.chat since "everyone" has an email address.

I often can't even get fairly technical folks (who write code by hand, etc) to use Element, even if I do all the server setup and just hand them the keys. It's too hard for most folk. It's too hard for me, and I've been maintaining my own matrix servers for 7+ years. I maintain 3 matrix servers right now. One synapse, and two continuwuity. NixOS makes it pretty easy to maintain servers, actually, as long as they're not open to the public.

And if anyone asks me "what should we use instead?", I'd probably say XMPP or IRC. And we know neither of those is perfect, either, and nothing open source and federated is as easy to onboard like Discord, Signal, or Slack.

But even though Element/Matrix sucks, it still works well enough for me to use it as my main communication. At least until I finish my own multi-protocol messenger. Which I started about 6 years ago and haven't had time to work on.

Disclosure: I wrote some of the code on Confide's backend back in 2021. I do not currently work at that company and am not promoting or un-promoting the app in any way.

comment_text.value:
He makes a key point in the FAQ section:

"Q: So when am I supposed to do my own job?

Answer: First, remember that your job, like all others, sits within a network of jobs - the output of others jobs is required for you to be able to do yours, while the output of your job is used as an input into other peoples' work.

Second, this focus-on-others'-success can be defined broadly: other people require you to do your job well so that they can use your output to do theirs well, so one basic requirement of ensuring the success of those around you is to make sure you do your own job well! See that guy over there next to you? Is he writing some code or working on some project that you're going to be dependent on? If he screws up, it's going to mess you up, right? Well, think about your own project - if you totally botch it, aren't there other people who are also depending on you to do it well and if you don't, their success will be inhibited? Well, don't let them down! Do your job well!"

It's been posted before https://hn.algolia.com/?q=http%3A%2F%2Falgeri-wong.com%2Fyis... but I came across it again after curating it in 2011 and was impressed by Yishan Wong's fundamental insights.

> Slow PR review

> Nitpicks on style, not substance

> Async waiting for review or re-review after making changes, harder to stay in what passes for a "flow state" nowadays

> A lot of a ceremony around straightforward changes

Those aren't great, but you what I like even less?

- Wall of nondeterministic bot text spam that may or may not be correct.

- Bot output has not been verified for correctness by the person who set up this bot output pipeline.

- Bot output has not even necessarily been read by the person who set it up.

- You have 24 hours to respond to this 5 page wall of text which may or may not be correct, or even make sense, or you will be penalized.

An appropriate response to this might be a reply flatly claiming that, actually, there aren't any problems after all, but that nobody has checked that that is true, and it is incumbent upon a human reviewer to verify your claims, like it was incumbent upon you to verify their bot's.

Can an LLM catch some errors? Absolutely. Can it be trusted to be correct absent review of the output? Absolutely not. So the simple solution seems to be, a human reviewer is free to run an LLM against code to review, on their own computer, and then they review the output, and they post the output only after verifying its correctness, taking personal responsibility for any issues with their posted output.

comment_text.value:
I feel for everyone in this situation. I don't think anyone is wrong to mourn the undeniably massive shift happening to something that has been such a big part of our lives, and I don't think anyone is wrong to be excited. I say this as someone who has worked in ML for coming up on 10 years now and is more towards the latter camp, where I love working with agents, and still spend plenty of time writing code by hand and studying. I don't think it's fair to pretend people are being unreasonable or are just "missing the big picture" for being unhappy.

But I also have found that where you work and what AI usage is like in your company is a pretty big deciding factor. Your comment, which I agree with, made me think about this. I consult a decent amount, and I've worked with companies where the engineering culture has adopted AI in a way I describe as "ugly." I should find a better word. But what I mean is that it's sort of like the attitude is "okay, now we can ship more tickets, so everyone take on 8x the workload". And they do a lot of "best practice" kind of stuff around using coding agents--every new anthropic article gets posted to slack, and there's always a new CI process for using agents--but they're fundamentally just trying to do the same work as before but kinda sorta faster. It's a weirdly miserable experience.

On the other hand, I've worked with companies where the engineering culture almost feels exuberant. I think a consistent difference is that in these companies, it feels like the engineers now have permission to try wildly ambitious things. It's not always optimally productive in the sense that more things get thrown away or end up just not really working out, but overall they move significantly faster and do more interesting work. Commonly, it's things they wanted to do before, but simply weren't realistic with their constraints around capacity. Or it's an idea like "this part of the codebase has always been a performance nightmare, but it's also a beast to untangle. I wonder if I could setup an autoresearch loop and let it run all day, even just to harvest some ideas?"

But yeah, when everyone sort of gives up and/or are forced to move an ungodly number of smaller tickets, it is a miserable time.

comment_text.value:
Probably a week ago someone posted a thread with the title "Why isn't the industry freaking out about DeepSeek 4.1 Flash?"

I have been intrigued about Chinese models for a long time, but never tried anything except an early Qwen. My daily driver was Luna, with occasional elevation to Terra or Sol - all on 5.6 as I found the output of 6 jarringly incomprehensible.

I still had 95 USD on my OpenRouter account, so I thought I would give DeepSeek Flash 4.1 a try.

I think now I can understand the person who created that thread.

Here is the setup I settled on, after a lot of refactoring and calibration of the workflow:

I have a "plan" prompt which explains to the agent (Luna) that I want to have a discussion about an idea I have in mind. The agent should use the Socratic method to pull out all the necessary info from me using pointed questions. When the agent feels it has a complete picture, it should elevate to a higher level model (Sol), and ask its review. If Sol has complaints, Luna keeps asking me until the points raised by Sol are clarified. The review rounds with Sol continue until Sol says "ready to implement".

At this point Luna creates four files in a directory I specify:

1. PLAN.md: the implementation plan with all the details that came out from the design discussion 2. PHASES.md: implementation phases 3. DECISIONS.md: design decisions (this serves the same role as ADRs aka. architectural decision records) 4. DIARY.md: append-only log of what happened during implementation

Files 2-4 are written by the implementing agent. Luna only adds headers to explain the purpose of the files.

Once these files are there, I start up a new Pi session, switch to Deepseek 4.1 Flash and then point it to this plan folder.

And then it goes brrrrr... :-)

Here is what I implemented in the past week using this method:

1. A capture/analysis/decompilation pipeline for C64 demos: I ask the agent to start a selected demo through VICE, and say "on" or "off" when I want it to start/stop capture. The capture process uses VICE's builtin trace functionality: the trace log is piped into Clojure where it is saved into an optimized binary format (chunks of trace events). Once I have everything captured, I unleash my analysis pipeline which checks the write patterns of the executed code: what it wrote (VIC, SID, CIA, memory) and when (rasterline, cycle). Then it splits the execution trace into segments by type deduced from the write patterns (decruncher, loader, raster, music) and then decompiles each segment into both traditional ASM files and a s-exp based syntax which roundtrips back into the in-memory representation. Once I have the results of the analysis pipeline, I can tell the agent to analyze any demopart and it can explain how the effects are built down to the tiniest timing detail. As a first test, I asked it to create a clean-room implementation of Fairlight's legendary intro and two days later I had it, with everything in sexp assembly, including the music routine and its data. (The reason it took so long was that this was the first decomp and it provided a lot of feedback to the pipeline development.) Finally I had it write an assembler, linker and packager which creates a PRG from the assembled and linked artifact, then runs it through VICE. Done.

2. A DSP compiler which lets me compile sexp forms of a C-like DSP language into native DSP kernels running on the JVM, JS and WASM. Currently I have about 600 tests which verify that the behavior of the three targets matches that of a reference interpreter written in Clojure. I have a full numeric tower with i32, f32, f64, support for arrays and structs, typical control flow constructs, and a library of DSP building blocks like oscillators, filters, LFOs, delays and a chorus effect. By the time this is ready (end of the weekend?), I will be able to build synthesizers like Synth1, Surge XT or Vital in Clojure/Script, compile the DSP kernels in the browser, choosing between JS or WASM backends, driving the kernels via AudioWorklets and sequencing them from the host language.

There are two power tools at play here:

1. Deepseek Flash 4.1 2. Clojure and ClojureScript

Deepseek is a BEAST. It just goes on and delivers, phase after phase. What it needs: clear instructions - this is covered by the planning process quite well, but I still find it needs some steering from time to time (the right nudget of wisdom dropped into its thought stream at the right moment works wonders)

And Clojure... well. That article PG wrote about LISP (Beating the averages): what I witness now proves all of those claims.

The agent LOVES Clojure. Especially the REPL (not so much the parentheses).

Winning strategy: give it two tools: start_jvm and clojure_eval. Implement everything else it may need - tools to start up HTTP servers, compile ClojureScript, add dependencies, capture a C64 demo, run Playwright via spel, etc. - as lightweight Clojure namespaces which provide APIs to all these functionality. Let these namespaces be thin: the namespace and the functions therein shall have docstrings which tell the agent what the functions do, but the functions themselves shall be lightweight proxies to the real implementations in sub-namespaces. Then point the agent to these top-level API namespaces via your AGENTS.md. Bam, instant discoverability with minimal context usage. It will do EVERYTHING through clojure_eval and the round-trip time will be phenomenal, a perfect match to the raw speed of the agent.

...

Now all I need to figure out is what will I do when all my dreams become manifest in flesh.

I built Panolayer because I wanted to feel in control of building software again. With complex architectures, thoughtful layers of abstractions, and trust in the stability of certain foundational layers. So when you add the 50th feature or make changes to the product, the code doesn’t silently break everywhere and become more buggy with every change.

Most of us build with agents now. But you quickly realize crafting prompts and asking agents to perform tasks, no matter how detailed, is basically like pulling the handle on a slot machine. You get a surprise of features, bugs, regressions, and unexpected refactors. Then you get those massive diffs, as if we all have time to look at +10,399, -4903 lines of changes, lol. It occurred to me that our coding tools weren’t designed for what our new jobs are, and a chat box was an overpivot that removed us from understanding and controlling the output.

So that's what I'm solving for with Panolayer: architecture as truth, comprehension of code, and a deterministic way for detecting regressions. All in one platform that brings those workflows together:

1.) Visual architecture that’s parsed directly from the source without LLM calls. You can jump right to the code from there.

2.) Verification Engine. It uses a custom model I built and deterministic rules. You see the regressions and can fix them before they get merged.

3.) One place for all the agents. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and others, working side by side with the same project context, in their own worktree. You can multitask work between them since not all agents are designed (or priced) for all tasks.

4.) Graphs. No one opens their harness, so I did because everyone should be able to customize it to whatever they’re working on. I made it easy, you can visually build them by dragging nodes onto the canvas and connecting them.

5.) A different take on diffs. Changes are shown on a spectrum from safe to risky, based on Panolayer’s findings, so you know where to look first.

6.) Living documents. I didn’t want to keep making docs that were outdated a week later. My agent already knows everything about the code so it should be able to generate them when prompted. And you shouldn’t have to worry if they’re out of date, they should just update.

Anyhow, I’ve never posted on HN before. It’s good to be here.

I’m just getting started, so Panolayer is free.

I’m curious what you all think. Good and bad, I’d love your feedback and hear how Panolayer could help keep your codebase more stable, while wrangling a bunch of agents in real-world codebases.

Not the GP poster, but some answers:

> Does SV40 cause cancer?

Yes, in a range of animal models at least.

SV40 can 'immortalise' cells, turning off regulatory functions which prevent uncontrolled division, which is an important part of carcinogenesis. This has been shown to contribute to cancer in experimental systems.

> Did and does SV40 inadvertendly inside the Polio Vaccine in the late 1950ies and 60ies cause cancer?

The evidence suggests not significantly, although it's impossible to rule out for some unlucky individuals.

The SV40-exposed cohorts rates of cancers don't differ that greatly from unexposed groups, so we can say with certainty that the rate is much less in humans than seen in laboratory systems. There were suggestions of differences for some cancers, but these are heterogeneous and often confounded, and the general consensus now seems to be the effect was small if not zero. I don't think there's a definitive answer on why - possibly the exposure was sufficiently low or the virus was not effective at infecting humans to significantly affect the carcinogenic processes.

> Does the Pfizer proces 2 SV40 promotor in the Covid Vaccine cause cancer?

Certainly not by the mechanism intact SV40 causes cancer.

That depends on the production of particular SV40 proteins which interfere with cell functions, which aren't present in that promoter.

> Does DNA contamination in general cause cancer?

In general, no.

Cells are constantly exposed to both native and foreign DNA fragments, and have plenty of mechanisms for dealing with them. Even if fragments were somehow incorporated and expressed, most are not inherently carcinogenic.

Hey HN, Marcus here.

I'm working on an agentic OS, which is much more than just a harness manager.

Meclaw is the foundation, the substrate, not a harness. Meclaw isn't based on a rigid harness structure arranged in a loop around an LLM. Meclaw breaks down a harness into its individual parts, into actors. Each actor is a directory, a config.json file, an SQLite database and a sandbox, and it doesn't access anything else. It's message-based. The edges between actors form a large graph. There are no direct agent loops. An LLM cell (cell=actor) makes a call and sends its response as a message. The conditional graph can then route the message wherever it needs to go, for example, to tools, and the route may, conditionally, lead back through the graph to the LLM, though it doesn't have to. It can also take its own paths, to another small, fast LLM, for instance, which first summarizes things before sending the message back to the original LLM. Everything is configurable. A change to the graph structure is made via a diff, which is posted to a system api, validated, and applied. All of this is written to a ledger in an audit-friendly manner during runtime. Everything is posted via the same interface.

Two things I find really exciting are the voice and web cells. I haven't seen either of them implemented this way directly in the harness yet. The voice cell is used to communicate with voice providers via WebSockets. In Meclaw-OS, I have an example that also connects to a FreeSwitch for telephony. Simply through a code cell. And the web cell is super exciting. It is SSR and pushes only small diffs to the client over a websocket. On the client side, I'm using the LiveView client from the Phoenix Project, thanks and best regards to Chris McCord. This gives agents the ability to dynamically display information to the user in realtime.

All of this is bundled with audit support, secrets are stored in a vault cell, and each cell runs in its own sandbox. It's all wrapped up nicely.

This is a follow-up post to https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49590351 because valid criticism was raised regarding the GH README, stating that it appears to be automatically generated. I have now completely rewritten it by hand.

Limitations, so no one wastes their time: Linux only, since isolation takes place at the kernel level (Landlock, network namespace, cgroup v2, seccomp), and while a macOS version would fulfill the promise, it would lose this feature. Code cells run Python 3, nothing else. No authentication in the binary, that belongs in the upstream proxy.

comment_text.value:
So, I think this article is circling something a lot more foundational when it comes to people’s disdain for AI. If you put more thought, more effort, and more originality into your work, you get something that starts to feel like an actual artistic expression. If you just type in a basic prompt and accept whatever comes back, that shows too. And I think that is a large part of why people feel insulted by this stuff in the first place.

It’s hard to respect a piece of work or take it seriously when it feels like the person who made it didn’t think it was worth giving much consideration. You’re asking someone to stop, look, and care about your poster and whatever it represents, but you haven’t given them much reason to believe you cared about it yourself. If you can’t take it seriously, how should we? It isn’t really about whether it took five minutes. It’s about whether there was any thought behind those five minutes.

So, I read this article as if it had the following title: “If you insist on using an LLM to generate visuals, you still have to put some thought into them.” But then, that starts to defeat the point for anyone who was using an LLM to avoid that effort in the first place, doesn’t it? You can make the process easier, but you can’t just assume that having produced something means you’ve made something worth sharing.

At the end of the day, I think there are valid uses for LLMs and there are uses that don’t add much of anything. As a consumer of content, the ones I respond to tend to be the ones where the LLM’s involvement isn’t the most obvious thing about the work. I want to see the person’s idea come through. A very light touch, not a deluge. This can absolutely apply to creating visuals, but it requires judgment, revision, and a willingness to do more than accept the first thing you’re given.

And it seems like a lot of people aren’t willing to put in that effort. That’s fine. Their work will continue to be distinguished by that lack of care, while people who are willing to put more into it will stand out. The initial novelty only carries something so far. Once you start picking up on the familiar patterns, that sense of something being slightly off becomes hard to ignore.

So, moving forward, I’m not so sure human creativity and input are things that can simply be outdone and made irrelevant. Maybe they’re an additional layer that keeps giving us somewhere further to go. An LLM can imitate what people have already brought to the table, but given access to that same LLM, we can bring our own experiences, ideas, and judgment into the mix. The tool gives us a starting point. I don’t see why we should assume it also determines how far we can take it.

The only ones that aren't horrible manage that because they're so bland there's nothing to go wrong. Look at an example with some detail, the "Now please make one in the style of a 90s drum n bass gig flyer, with early 3D/fractal computer imagery" poster.

At the top of the page we have a deformed wireframe sphere. A wireframe sphere is stylistically appropriate, but the incorrect rendering is not. The "CGI" aesthetic requires obviously computer generated lines, which in the 90s meant accurate and regular lines.

Next we have a messed-up stellated polyhedron, and a messed-up dot pattern. These also fail for the same reason. The main 3D rendering is also obviously broken, as are many other small details.

But the biggest failure is the complete misunderstanding of the culture. 90s DnB was absolutely not about "good vibes". The smiley face logo is completely inappropriate; that's associated with late 80s/early 90s rave culture, pre-DnB era. 90s DnB was much darker and edgier in tone. The scene was almost exclusively male, and it maintained a aggressive vibe carried over from jungle.

A 90s DnB event would never advertise "bringing communities together". Audiences would be repelled by such messaging. This is despite it actually doing just that, as the scene was racially integrated in a way that mainstream music at the time was not. If there's going to be pro-social messaging on the poster it has to be there only implicitly.

Not really. We use -logy to mean science or study of something. Philosophy with no other prefix is study of the Self, in a general sense, because Knowledge is a personal thing.

Science and Religion is a common division among intelligent beings. Sometimes they move forward differently in our minds singularly, and collectively.

You can accept truths like learning, knowledge, roles, collective intelligence, etc., and all the depth of the Science that goes with it, and still use those ideas at a high level in order to to predict future events, to do something 'useful'.

Google just posted a white paper about RSI 'dreaming'.

You take some super complex thing and reduce it within the scope of something bigger. Then you let an observer (self) recursively pick and choose the reduced scopes (like steps in a plan), and by observation of outcomes, pick the 'better path' for the future. It's like dreaming and reflection, considering past and future, and then choosing to learn in a direction that helps you change the future.

By picking and choosing in this way: you can learn and grow into shapes that help you predict the future again and again, to persist.

It's a loop within a loop, and that's neat to me (Cybernetics comes to mind). And so the author's idea tugs at me, because if we really do live in a Black Hole, what's at the end? A spikey but supremely ordered state, yet still a Singularity. What's at the beginning of the Big Bang? Also a Singularity, but extremely smooth. What's in the 'singularity' that is our moment right now: just our minds. The only thing that comes to mind is the 'you', the collective experience that defines your moment.

If you loosely connect the idea of a Big Bang being the beginning, and a Black hole being the end:

At one end: a single idea (low entropy, smooth ordered state: only on predictable event comes next, expansion), at another, many (high entropy, many predictable states if you consider the start, but always the same ending).

Intelligence is about predicting the state of one moment to the other, in order to do something useful about the future.

There's discussions and disruptions in Mathematics about: what makes a 'valid' Math proof? Do we accept only Human understanding, or Machines? Right now we've accepted Human only. The only way it matters, is if the discovery of proof is useful to someone or something.

Imagine an AI proofs out this author's work: If every single AI agreed, would you accept it? Or is AI actually a waste of 'Time' and we should stop using it. Is there beauty in Logic the way Dirac looks at Math?

As it is, we're waiting on some Humans to dig through Math and proof out and 'understand' in some areas, but not in others. We measure the utility of AI: how much time does it save, which means it's a very personal measure.

When it comes time to do this exercise where Science and Religion meet: we don't know if we should 'trust' an AI's understanding of Math over our own. We measure its utility differently in some areas than others...and so it becomes a very personal subject and is my 'stuff' to believe. My personal truth, as gross as it is. My 'shit to believe'.

To end this argument on a spiritual note that is also grounded in personal truth: consider loops once again.

And this time, probably the most important agent, the outer loop that matters most: Your beginning, and your ending. Your moment, is a collection of choices you make based on your own personal observation.

Whatever you believe: prepare for your own ending properly. Criticize when you feel it's proper, and help, when you see fit. Your choices.

popups make alt F4

..rather than increasing noise across the whole of HN. this rule is closely related to another site rule: "use the best possible interpretation of the parent comment" because it too is a rule that is in place as an attempt to steer toward "curious discussion" (high S/N ratio)

comment_text.value:
There's a fundamental difference between procedurally generated worlds and how Spore actually works.

The creatures, vehicles, and buildings weren't generated -- they were created by other players and exchanged asynchronously, then seeded into your procedurally generated galaxy.

Spore is a Massively Single Player Online Game: no real-time multiplayer, but your galaxy fills with other people's content.

That's the opposite of the oatmeal problem. Procgen gives you infinite bowls that all taste the same. Spore gave you a finite but large set of bowls, each made by someone who cared about it. Different tradeoff, different failure mode -- but not the one this thread is about.

GDC 2005, Will Wright, The Future Of Content:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N4ScRG_reIw

>[...] Also I want to apologize for the title of this talk in the description, which I know was kind of hopelessly vague.

>What usually happens every year is GDC, they call me up, and they say "we want you to do a talk" and I say okay, and then a week later they say "what's your talk about" and so then I think about it for a while and oh, get a rough idea of what I'm going to talk about, and I give them some kind of generic title in that area.

>That's what usually happens. But this year was different. This year when they asked me what I was going to talk about, I just flat out lied.

>But, so I'm not really going to talk about the future of content. I'm really more in fact going to talk about a possible future of content you know.

>It seems like the theme that I'm coming away from this conference with so far is that the next generation titles are going to be incredibly expensive, we're going to have to build mountains of content, and it's going to drive most of the smaller players out of the market.

>And I'd like to offer potentially an alternate vision of that. You know I think that there is a way to deal with that more creatively. So maybe a more accurate title for this talk would be "What I learned about content from The Sims".

That was 21 years ago. The same argument is being made again right now, with a different machine offered as the answer, and Will's alternative is still the one nobody is trying.

Will's advice for game designers and creative humans in general, from my notes on the talk:

>If you have a weird idea that's so outside of the box, don't forget it. You should go back and revisit your weird ideas later, because you can never know where they might lead to.

In February 2007 PopSci, Will explains the whole design rationale:

https://www.popsci.com/entertainment-gaming/article/2007-02/...

>We thought about it. In fact, technically, based on all the stuff we've already done for it, it wouldn't be very hard at all. We've already solved all the hard problems we would need to do a persistent online world version of Spore. The hard part is, what happens when you come to a planet and the planet's offline? Which would be the case. In fact, one of the reasons why I kind of went down this path is that nobody has really explored the hybrid model. And this really is a hybrid, it's what we call a massively single-player game, where we try to get the benefits of an online game, which is all the people building the world collectively together, without the liabilities, which is that the 14-year-old can kill you or that you've invested all this time in your planet and somebody comes along and blows it up, and therefore you had to put everybody on the same level treadmill. And I hate these level treadmill games, and I wanted the players to feel really empowered.

GDC 2005 Report: The Future of Content

https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/gdc-2005-report-the-fut...

I posted more details on the Spore Stats discussion in 2023:

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36280275

>Here are my notes and summary of the GDC 2005 talk where Will Wright first revealed Spore, which I asked Will to review and check for accuracy. It's interesting to compare the design he described in the talk with what Maxis eventually shipped. Video of the hour long talk:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N4ScRG_reIw

>One of the essential problems with designing a Massively Multi Player Online Game like Spore is that players at different levels of the simulation run at different time scales.

>Maintaining time synchronization between players is also the reason The Sims Online doesn't have a "Pause" button or speed controls, or automatically pause in build and buy mode, like The Sims.

>So instead, Spore is a Massively Single Player Online Game. Users don't interact with each other in real time, but instead users can create their own content, and it exchanges that content between users asynchronously.

>That's also how The Sims Exchange lets players asynchronously upload and download their Sims save files along with web pages describing their house, sims, and photo album.

https://donhopkins.medium.com/the-future-of-content-will-wri...

>The Future of Content — Will Wright’s Spore Demo at GDC 3/11/2005

>What I learned about content from the Sims. …and why it’s driven me to procedural methods. …And what I now plan to do with them. Talk by Will Wright, Game Developers Conference, 3/11/2005.

>Based on notes taken by Don Hopkins at the talk, and other discussions and review by Will Wright. The title of the talk “The Future of Content” was purposefully vague, because Will wanted to show Spore in public for the first time, but he had to flat out lie about the title and send a fake set of slides for the EA executives to review, so they didn’t know what he was about to do. A more accurate title for the talk would be “What I Learned About Content from The Sims, and Why it’s Driven Me to Procedural Methods, and What I Now Plan to Do With Them”. [...]

>Wired asked for an illustration to print in the magazine, anything he wanted. So he made a diagram of Spore that Wired published, but he didn’t tell them what it was. The design docs for Spore have been out in Wired Magazine for a year now. (It’s in the Feb 2004 issue of Wired.)

>Will’s Secret Diagram of Spore published in February 2004 Wired:

https://donhopkins.com/home/WiredSporeDiagram.jpg

[...]

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36280831

>And that is the whole point, how you win the game: become involved with the content creation community!

>The powerful but easy to use direct manipulation editor tools, the automatic content sharing system, and the online community around user created content, were together the most innovative and successful things about Spore. (As contrasted with the not as well realized gameplay and storytelling design goals.) [...]

>Chaim Gingold, A Brief History of Spore:

http://www.levitylab.com/blog/2011/02/brief-history-of-spore...

>Creativity

>Of course, these aren’t any old aliens we ask players to invest in — they’re your creation, your aliens. Once you start customizing, and design your creature, emotional investment is generated. It’s magic. Even the ugly ones are loved by their parents. Many games thrive on the interest generated by players’ creative investment. Console role playing games, for example, get this effect when players invest time in equipping and naming characters. I’ve always felt more attached to my characters as I fuss over their outfits and equipment. Creative interaction seems to always generate emotional involvement and attachment. Psychologically, it would seem that part of this stems from the sunk cost fallacy — we become attached to things we’ve invested time and energy into. Of course, it’s not just the hundreds of hours invested in a World of Warcraft character, their relationships, and possessions that generate attachment, it’s the sense that our fabrications are extensions of ourselves. As recipients of our attention and creative energy, our handiworks are reflections of who we are, tangible manifestations of our personalities. It’s no wonder we become attached to what we make, and take the success or failure of our own work and ideas very personally.

>Spore neatly solves the alien attachment problem by asking the player to design them. If a player makes a creature, and it’s appealing, they’ll be quite invested in it. Reflecting on the success of The Sims Exchange, where players shared stories, characters, houses, and objects for The Sims, Will realized that shared creativity would give Spore a broader appeal. Why not build creative exchange into the game, rather than as a website that orbits it? Player created assets are constantly being uploaded and downloaded by Spore, enough material to fill a galaxy. There’s nothing like taking home your latest finger painting, and having mom hang it on the fridge for everyone to see. Sharing not only fills up the galaxy with cool stuff, but allows the entire world to see your fridge, motivating you to continue creating.

>Of course, a lot of deep magic must work properly for something like Spore’s creature creator to function properly. It must be natural to use, easily producing satisfying results for anyone, from beginners to advanced users. And these aliens, lumps of polygons that no animator has ever seen before, must be brought to life. These are rather complicated endeavors, from a design, aesthetic, and technical point of view, but the player should never notice any of it. The game design implications are also challenging — the game must be playable and interesting, regardless of the creatures dropped into it.

I spent about an hour looking at the code and found some glaring issues that should be fixed before trusting it with real money.

- Yahoo News is introduced twice (sentiment and news analysis) which double weights it

- Sentiment analysis prompt primes the model to be bullish on Nvidia.

- In the self learning loop there is a complex parsing bug that results in hallucinated memories when agents return truncated responses

- You can completely control sentiment analysis of a subreddit by simply maintaining a majority of the 5 most recently posted messages, regardless of any quality metric

- The reflection prompt states the agent must cite alpha, which in a market wide downturn causes it to think correctly placed calls were losses

The only thing that makes sense to me at this point is that this was an SNI bypass. By using either `/etc/hosts` or `curl --resolve` like this:

  curl -k \
  --resolve bypass.blob.core.windows.net:443:20.223.25.152 \
  -H 'Host: wabi-north-europe-i-primary-api.analysis.windows.net' \
  ... \
  https://bypass.blob.core.windows.net/...
That will cause `curl` to make a connection to 20.223.25.152:443 with a ClientHello SNI=bypass.blob.core.windows.net. Presumably this connection is then allowed to continue. The server is likely going to send back the wrong certificate, thus the `-k`, but then the HTTP Host header selects the correct server.

So that all fits. What doesn't make sense is that these agents were allegedly running in Azure and AFAICT this isn't sufficient to bypass Azure network restrictions/firewall which enforces that the SNI hostname matches the destination IP by doing the DNS resolution on the SNI hostname itself.

In any case, the environment should be blocking all outbound port 80/443 connections except to the proxy or to Azure Block Storage. But it seems that's not the case, that `curl` is able to connect directly to 20.223.25.152:443, and that maybe something else is doing SNI filtering that's more easily fooled than Azure firewall. Certainly some firewalls are (or have been) susceptible to SNI bypass:

https://dl.ifip.org/db/conf/im/im2015exp/137348.pdf

There are more-or-less two possibilities: either he believes that the election was stolen despite the total absence of evidence to that effect, in which case he is a fool; or he cynically pretends to believe that for the purpose of personal gain, in which case he is a liar and a con-man. comment_text.value:
It's an amazing and disingenuous posit that the problem here lies with the Algorithm as opposed to the consequences under which it was introduced - cost-cutting. The barriers to care for patients who are already struggling with serious mental conditions are not a new phenomenon related to automated tooling derived from best practice corpus. Rather, they are a direct result of a decline in triage staffing.

Take cardiologist Dr. Lee Goldman’s chest pain decision-making algorithm, originally devised at Cook County Hospital to diagnose heart attacks.

Effectively a poster in the ER illustrating a simple decision tree, it outperformed traditional doctor diagnoses; achieving over 95% accuracy and proving 70% better at identifying patients not having a heart attack. This landmark clinical protocol represented a quantum-leap in outcomes, eventually refined to the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) used as the gold-standard today.

So not only are algorithmic approaches old-hat in clinical settings, they are in fact a core component of contemporary best practice medicine. But that's somewhat besides the point when much of the issues raised in the article above refer to issues of executive dysfunction - areas in which low-context Agentic AI are basically designed to remedy, e.g.

// Instead of being referred directly by primary care doctors and contacted to schedule appointments, patients were routed through an app, nonclinical call center staff or simply given a phone number to call. “Now the onus is on the patients to be their own care coordinators,” she said... This dynamic can be particularly challenging for some patients. “Lack of motivation and lack of follow-through are the most common symptoms of depression on the planet,”

So the answer here is clearly an increase in appropriate AI resources, rather than throwing the baby out with the bathwater. If we trust a decision-tree poster to do cardiovascular triage better than the instincts of cardiovascular specialists, and OCR models to interpret results better than veteran Radiologists, why not Agentic AI to do the basic work of scheduling appointments?

comment_text.value:
Let me give you long-haul bicycle travel as an example: back when there was an active blogging scene, people sharing route tips and bike-build breakdowns could be sure that a decent amount of other people would find it and benefit from it: the blogs got picked up by search engines and were readily findable, and there was still a culture of using the open web.

Today, no one you will see the content that you posted to help other people out. Google began deprioritizing personal blogs a decade ago already, and now a whole generation has come up that doesn't know the open web is a thing. When people look for tips in this hobby, it is overwhelmingly on phone apps like Komoot or PolarSteps, on the general image-based social media like YouTube or Instagram, or (already for an older-skewing crowd that still uses browsers) on the big for-profit website Bikepacking.com that grew by using its SEO-fu to wipe out the non-profit-driven scene.

There is a community around this hobby, one with a lot of IRL interaction, and people do enjoy that feeling of community. But claiming that people "aren't really your peer" if they don't use the old open web that we knew, is just cutting yourself off from that.

Ah, I think I know this one. It's because people who make their own guns are nerds. You know, like you or I, except in a different topic. I remember reading a couple of posts on R*dd*t where two folk were discussing fitting accessories to guns and one posted something like "No, you can fit that, all you do is mill a slot on top of the receiver and drill and tap a hole at the end and you can just about screw this thing in place" kind of thing.

I read the discussion and thought "yeah that's nerd talk, just not about analogue synthesizers, old Landrover gearboxes, or Pascal compilers".

I guess the reason for blocking 3D printers from making gun parts is because it's easier than doing it "by hand". All you really need to do is get a copy of the files from someone who has them, print it out in something suitable, and you have viable gun components with very little "real work" involved.

By contrast here in the UK, where it's quite surprising what you're allowed to own and operate if you comply with the laws (here you're allowed fully automatic weapons, if you keep them at a suitable shooting range and don't try to wander around town with them, and you're not oh maybe a convicted violent criminal for example) one of my late father's friends was a gunsmith. My dad was an excellent machinist, and so he made some components for his friend, and I remember standing in the machine shop where they worked while he turned a chamber for a gun his colleague was building in the lathe. "There you go," he said, taking it out of the chuck, "that's legal".

Then he took it over to the mill, and cut a couple of holes and slots that would allow it to actually function as a chamber, "And there - now it's *illegal*."

Then, as he handed it to his friend, who was licensed to have "home made" gun parts, to stamp his initials on, "And now it's legal again."

Of course since people aren't allowed to just walk around with handguns since the school shooting, it's all a little more difficult - but the police will tell you what you need to do to keep it legal.

It's still slightly easier to get a shotgun licence than a motorcycle licence here.

comment_text.value:
> That's a rather bold claim.

No, it's not a bold claim. It's a strong consensus among people working on privacy and security engineering or research.

> Care to elaborate?

We did in our response to you at https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49366321 and posted more elsewhere. Others have posted far more details about it in articles and papers.

> I think you are somewhat conflating the needs of desktop/laptop/mobile users.

No, we aren't. Desktops need far better privacy and security than they have today. That does not require giving up functionality. Development can be done in contained hardware accelerated virtual machines specific to projects. It doesn't require running an OS where anything goes and software doesn't run in a sandbox on the host. QubesOS could have a far more secure OS as the one people interact with despite running far less secure operating systems in many of the guests. It would not prevent people getting work done. It can also be done with far higher usability than is currently provided.

> Hardware security tied to unlocking modes makes little sense on desktops.

Verified boot and hardware support for disk encryption is very valuable to a desktop and laptop.

> I can lose my phone, or possibly my laptop, but my servers and workstation are at home, guarded by a dog and a shotgun.

Servers and workstations being in a trusted location doesn't mean the security of those against physical attacks doesn't matter. It also doesn't address remote attacks.

> Disk encryption already covers a realistic threat model such as a break-in.

You do not have comparable disk encryption. You have it in a form that only truly works when the device hasn't had the encryption passphrase entered since boot. It's wide open to data extraction via a bunch of debugging interfaces. There's incredibly poor security against physical attacks at both a hardware and OS level.

> I don't expect protection against apps, and don't want to pay the performance tax that comes with "enhanced" memory allocators and memory-safe languages/runtimes.

The performance cost of exploit protections can be determined in a granular way. GrapheneOS has a toggle to use the standard allocator for any apps. Memory safe languages do not imply inherent overhead and can be faster for some uses. Rust is very high performance and even Java can be higher performance for certain uses where there are lots of short lived allocations.

> The irony is that Android is practically designed to run commercial malware. The sandbox you have in mind does very little in practice.

Android's sandbox provides enormous benefits and the permission model gets significantly better ever year. Android has heavily focused on improving a lot of what you're talking about itself upstream and GrapheneOS improves it much more.

Android can force backwards incompatible changes on the whole app ecosystem to improve privacy and security which it does with each new major target SDK version for the major yearly releases. They limit how much they do this in each major release and aren't as focused on privacy and security as us so we wish they did more, but no other mainstream platform has made such substantial improvements to the privacy and security model for apps. Android has improved drastically more than iOS since it had a much worse starting point and had to catch up. It has caught up in most areas and surpassed iOS in some but still needs improvements in others. GrapheneOS is heavily focused on those areas where it's still behind iOS and has done a lot to improve it.

> Users consent to sharing files, contacts, locations, photos, when asked to because they want to use some app, and all of that is sent straight to Facebook, Google, or others.

GrapheneOS has Contact Scopes and Storage Scopes to choose which contacts and files/media are shared with the app seeing it as the permissions it requested being granted. This is an extension of Android's standard approach built on the infrastructure it provides for this. It's already heavily moving in this direction and has increasingly forced apps to use a case-by-case consent approach. Location, Microphone and Camera access in Android can be granted on a one-time basis. It heavily pushes apps to using the system file picker, media picker, contact picker, etc. and store policy is increasingly used as a deterrent against requesting bulk access. GrapheneOS does much better and it's able to do much better because of the infrastructure Android provides.

> Android apps can also communicate in some obscure and unexpected ways to discover each other and share information behind the user's back

Communication better apps is possible within profiles where both apps want to engage in it. Users do have the ability to prevent apps seeing each other and communicating via profiles (Private Spaces, work profiles and secondary users). GrapheneOS will be providing finer-grained nested profiles beyond a single Private Space per user or a single work profile along with it being more convenient.

Apps getting access to user data in the first place is what's most relevant rather than whether they can communicate regardless. They could also send it to a service rather than another app. Android is focused on preventing apps getting access to sensitive data including data from other apps or the user's profile data (files, media, contacts, etc.) which GrapheneOS greatly enhances. We do have things like a Network toggle but it's not intended as a substitute for the main approach of avoiding apps getting access to sensitive data. Android is currently phasing in a standard local network access permission for apps will provide one of the main benefits of our Network toggle.

Android can force backwards incompatible changes on the whole app ecosystem to improve privacy and security which it does with each new major target SDK version for the major yearly releases. They limit how much they do this in each major release and aren't as focused on privacy and security as us so we wish they did more, but no other mainstream platform has made such substantial improvements to the privacy and security model for apps. Android has improved drastically more than iOS since it had a much worse starting point and had to catch up. It has caught up in most areas and surpassed iOS in some but still needs improvements in others. GrapheneOS is heavily focused on those areas where it's still behind iOS and has done a lot to improve it.

> Users consent to sharing files, contacts, locations, photos, when asked to because they want to use some app, and all of that is sent straight to Facebook, Google, or others.

GrapheneOS has Contact Scopes and Storage Scopes to choose which contacts and files/media are shared with the app seeing it as the permissions it requested being granted. This is an extension of Android's standard approach built on the infrastructure it provides for this. It's already heavily moving in this direction and has increasingly forced apps to use a case-by-case consent approach. Location, Microphone and Camera access in Android can be granted on a one-time basis. It heavily pushes apps to using the system file picker, media picker, contact picker, etc. and store policy is increasingly used as a deterrent against requesting bulk access. GrapheneOS does much better and it's able to do much better because of the infrastructure Android provides.

> Android apps can also communicate in some obscure and unexpected ways to discover each other and share information behind the user's back

Communication better apps is possible within profiles where both apps want to engage in it. Users do have the ability to prevent apps seeing each other and communicating via profiles (Private Spaces, work profiles and secondary users). GrapheneOS will be providing finer-grained nested profiles beyond a single Private Space per user or a single work profile along with it being more convenient.

Apps getting access to user data in the first place is what's most relevant rather than whether they can communicate regardless. They could also send it to a service rather than another app. Android is focused on preventing apps getting access to sensitive data including data from other apps or the user's profile data (files, media, contacts, etc.) which GrapheneOS greatly enhances. We do have things like a Network toggle but it's not intended as a substitute for the main approach of avoiding apps getting access to sensitive data. Android is currently phasing in a standard local network access permission for apps will provide one of the main benefits of our Network toggle.

The poster is implying the reinforcement at play is the problematic thing at issue, and they are assigning the word "gambling" to represent it, or so it looks like to me. I think you aren't parsing their meaning correctly because what they seem to be aiming for is extinguishing the automatic reinforcement.

You're claiming it's making your life better, ostensibly by a relative report of the hedonic response a newly introduced piece of music auto delivered to you by the recommendation algorithm invokes. The problem they hint at though is the passive nature involved. You aren't finding that new piece, it's getting pushed. That pushing incentivizes optimizing for continued engagement, an act children, intellectually and developmentally disabled individuals, as well as those in the throes of cognitive decline/impairment, are not at all well equipped to self-regulate against when pitted against paid behavioral psychologists designing maximally engagement encouraging interfaces.

The incentive, and the existence of predatible populations is the problem I take away from it. I can agree you should be free to opt-in mind, but I can also see the wisdom in a by default interface wherein engagement hacking is forbidden being the norm, and that norm coming with a minimally controversial algorithm boiling down to "chronological feed of known/subscribed to sources", followed by a link of some sort to open an interface to the recommendations.

Facebook/Insta/Shorts are absolutely not that non-engagement farming interface. Hell my grandmother toward the end was about driven mad by it, and it was all I could do to just try to remind her that just because the machine had it on offer doesn't mean she had to partake, but her community centric character made that a bit of an ordeal for her.

There is absolutely a pathological pattern to the way tech companies hunt for eyeballs to monetize, and it is a damn shame it's taken this long to start getting traction to even talk about it.

comment_text.value:
I think the main reason many people (including me), very often, lack the motivation to read content that is likely generated by AI is the suspicion that it comes from a place of intellectual laziness. Another reason, based on personal experience, is that AI content may suffer from too much verbosity, too much jargon and over-confidence, which makes the reading experience feel fake and border-line irritating. In many cases the content may have very little to no nuance, which is ultimately a waste of time. As an anecdote, someone posted a blogpost on Linkedin on using agents to implement a driver to access PCIe devices over TCP/IP. I was intrigued because that's not an easy task for several reasons, like handling PCIe interrupts and DMA. For exmaple, how does the remote machine map the device's PCIe BARs? And when it issues I/O to the devices registers, how are these reads and writes transferred to the remote device. In the end, this is just some virtual memory. In a local machine, this is either directly mapped to the PCIe physical addresses or some IOMMU virtual address space which is then translated by the hardware upon CPU/device/VM access.

After reading the long verbose promising article, in the end, the guy (with the help of the agent) only managed to implement access to the PCIe config space so that lspci on the remote machine works and shows the remote PCIe device, but that's all. It never addressed the issues above nor even mentioned them. The code was AI generated. The article was AI-written. The article never made a reference to DMA, interrupts, MSIX-X, IOMMU, IOTLB, virtual memory, etc, but it made big claims on next-gen datacenter disaggregated architecture, boosting GPU utilization, reducing large scale inference costs, etc.

Anyway, you get my point: big long beautiful words, but zero nuance.

story_title.value: AI;DR (AI; Didn't Read)
